newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL GOV'T PLANS TO SELL PETROBRAS VOTING SHARES.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL GOV'T PLANS TO SELL PETROBRAS VOTING SHARES.

text.p: Brazil's government plans to sell roughly one third of the ordinary shares it holds in state-owned oil giant Petrobras now that a new law regulating the oil and gas industry allows for the sale, a Petrobras official said.
The official, who did not want to be named, said the sale could earn the government as much as $6.3 billion.
"The government has decided to sell, but it hasn't decided when," he said. "It could still be this year, but more probably next year."

Under the new petroleum law, which was signed by President Fernando Henrique Cardoso on Wednesday and which opens Brazil's oil and gas industry to private competition, the government is obliged to retain only 50 percent plus one share of Petrobras ordinary share capital.
Currently, the government has an 81.72 percent stake in the oil giant's voting capital.
And for the first time ever, the new petroleum law also allows ordinary shares in Petrobras to be sold to foreigners.

The Petrobras official said Brazil's National Development Bank (BNDES) would be in charge of designing and carrying out the share sale, which would probably take the form of a global offer in which individual investors are limited as to how much they can buy.

"Investors will probably be limited to buying only a very small amount each, given that any one shareholder who has a voting stake of five percent or more could appoint a director to the company," he said. "That is not what the government wants. It doesn't want anybody else having any say in the company."

He said the money from the share sale would probably be used to pay off Brazil's debts, as is the case with most privatization receipts, but the government might also invest some of the money back in Petrobras.
The government currently owes Petrobras around $7 billion in oil and alcohol subsidies which have accumulated over the last 20 years, he added.

The official said Petrobras was keen to issue a Level 3 American Depositary Receipt (ADR) as soon as possible, but the subject of government debt had to be resolved first given the prerequisites for listing Level 3 ADRs on the New York Stock Exchange.
